title: Looking closely and noticing changes
keyIdea: Scientists look closely and notice what changes. Say what it was like before and what it is like now. Some changes are fast, like ice melting. Some are slow, like a banana going brown.

kid: Put ice in a cup. Wait. Look again! The ice is water now. Before it was hard. Now it is wet.
Look at a banana each day. First it is yellow. Then it gets spots. Now it is brown.
A magnifier makes small things look big. Look up close. You may see a tiny bug or a seed.
Some things change fast. Some change slow. Some do not change at all. Look and say what you see.
adult: At three and four, science is mostly careful looking. Children use their senses to notice details, compare two things, and say how something changed over time. Development Matters asks three and four year olds to talk about the differences between materials and changes they notice, and the early learning goal for the natural world asks them to explore and describe what they see.

Give your child the words of observation: before and now; first, then and now; the same and different; bigger and smaller. A hand lens, or magnifier, makes small details easy to see. Looking at the same thing a few times shows that some changes are fast, like ice melting in about an hour on a warm day, and some are slow, like a banana going brown over several days.

Common mistakes to watch for: thinking melted ice has gone away, when it has turned into the water in the cup; thinking a changed thing is a new thing; noticing only big changes and missing small ones; and mixing up which picture came first. Each time, ask: what was it like before, and what is it like now?

In the lab your child slides time on to melt ice, spots three changes between a Before and a Now picture, and notices what stayed the same. Then they move a magnifier over an apple slice to find tiny things, step through an hour, a day and a week, and put pictures in first, then, now order.

familyTip: Put an apple slice and an ice cube on two plates. Look at them now, after lunch and at bedtime. Ask what is different now from before, and draw or photo each one to compare.

visual.caption: Did it change? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: watch ice melt, spot what changed, look up close with a magnifier, see fast and slow changes, and order pictures first, then, now.

practice.prompt: Ice sits in a warm cup. Later the cup has water and no ice. What happened?
practice.hint: Where did the water in the cup come from?
practice.explain: The ice melted. It turned into the water in the cup, so it did not go away.

practice.prompt: Mia checks a banana for {n} days. First yellow, then spots. What comes next?
practice.hint: Bananas get darker as they get older, not lighter.
practice.explain: Next it goes brown all over. After {n} days or so, a banana keeps getting browner; it does not go back.

practice.prompt: Which tool helps you see a tiny seed in an apple?
practice.hint: Which tool makes small things look big?
practice.explain: A magnifier, also called a hand lens, makes tiny things look big so you can see the detail.

practice.prompt: Leo looks at a puddle at {n} o’clock and again after lunch. It is smaller. What can he say?
choices: Before it was big, now it is small
practice.hint: Use before and now to say what is different.
practice.explain: Before it was big, now it is small. Saying before and now describes the change Leo saw since {n} o’clock.

pool.prompt: Which changes faster in the sun?
pool.hint: Think about which one you can watch change before lunch.
pool.explain: An ice cube melts fast, in about an hour in the sun. A banana takes days and a rock does not change.

pool.prompt: Before, the flower was shut. Now it is open. Is it the same flower?
pool.hint: Did someone swap it, or did the same flower open up?
pool.explain: Yes, it is the same flower. It changed by opening up.

pool.prompt: Ava looks at a leaf and a teddy at {n} o’clock and again at bedtime. The teddy is the same. Is that OK to say?
choices: Yes, some things stay the same
pool.hint: Noticing what stays the same is part of looking closely.
pool.explain: Yes. Good scientists say what changed and what stayed the same, like Ava did from {n} o’clock to bedtime.

pool.prompt: Put these in order: white apple slice, a bit brown, very brown. Which is first?
pool.hint: The slice gets browner the longer it is left out.
pool.explain: The white slice is first. Then it goes a bit brown, and now it is very brown.

pool.prompt: How can you see small things on a bug?
choices: Look up close with a magnifier
pool.hint: Which way makes tiny details big?
pool.explain: Look up close with a magnifier. A quick look from far away misses small details.

pool.prompt: Sam has {n} ice cubes in a bowl. After a while they are gone and the bowl has water. Where did the ice go?
pool.hint: What is in the bowl now that was not there before?
pool.explain: It melted. All {n} ice cubes turned into the water in the bowl.

pool.prompt: Which words tell about a change?
pool.explain: Before and now, or first, then and now, help you say what changed over time.

pool.prompt: A puddle is big in the morning and gone at night. What happened?
pool.hint: Compare morning and night. What is different?
pool.explain: It dried up. The puddle got smaller and smaller until it was gone.
